title: Design & Innovation — Chapter 2: IoT and Blockchain
subtitle: EPITA D&I4DBT Class 2. Concept-focused questions on IoT fundamentals, protocols and 5G, architecture and security, use cases, network economics and standards, blockchain fundamentals, applications, adoption challenges, and the IoT+Blockchain value chain. Emphasis on reasoning and situational understanding.

questions.question: Today's Internet first underwent convergence (TV, radio, telecom, web all moving onto it) and is now described as diverging. Why is this divergence happening?
options: Network bandwidth is shrinking, forcing services to separate onto dedicated infrastructures
Present-day technology adoption pushes distinct domains (social networks, cloud, data indexing, IoT) to specialize and grow apart
Regulators have legally mandated separation of services into isolated networks
The Internet is becoming offline as physical media regain dominance
questions.explanation: The slides frame convergence (everything coming onto the Internet) as the past trend, and divergence as the current one: as adoption matures, specialized domains such as social networks, cloud computing, content/data indexing and emerging IoT differentiate and expand. Bandwidth is increasing not shrinking, and the divergence is driven by adoption dynamics, not regulation or a return offline.

questions.question: The single feature that most distinguishes IoT from the traditional human-centric Internet is the ability to:
options: Compress data more efficiently for faster downloads
Transfer data over a network without requiring human-to-human or human-to-computer interaction
Store all records permanently in a central database
Encrypt every message end to end
questions.explanation: IoT centers on devices that exchange data autonomously, without human-to-human or human-to-computer interaction. Compression, central storage and encryption may be present but are not the defining property; the defining property is machine autonomy in data transfer.

questions.question: M2M (machine-to-machine) communication is presented as communication between entities that do not necessarily need direct human intervention. Why is that autonomy strategically important for IoT?
options: It removes the need for any network infrastructure
It allows decision and communication processes to be automated at a scale humans could not manually sustain
It guarantees that no data is ever collected about people
It makes every device cheaper than a barcode
questions.explanation: ETSI frames M2M services as intended to automate decision and communication processes. The value is automation at scale: billions of devices acting and coordinating without manual mediation. M2M still requires networks, still can collect personal data, and says nothing about device cost.

questions.question: Why are unique identifiers (UIDs) treated as a foundational requirement in IoT systems?
options: They encrypt the data payload carried by each device
They allow each of a vast number of devices to be individually addressed so data can be attributed and routed
They reduce the energy consumption of sensors
They replace the need for any communication protocol
questions.explanation: With huge numbers of interrelated devices, each must be uniquely addressable so data can be attributed to and routed from the right thing. UIDs are about identity and addressing, not encryption, power saving, or replacing protocols.

questions.question: IoT is characterized in the summary as a 'data generation technology set' rather than a single technology. What is the reasoning behind that characterization?
options: It refers to a single standardized protocol adopted worldwide
It combines several distinct technologies — RFID, sensors, smart technologies, nanotechnology — that together generate data
It is purely a software layer with no hardware component
It is defined by one dominant vendor's platform
questions.explanation: The slides describe IoT as a set that combines RFID, sensors, smart technologies and nano-technologies to generate data across supply chains. It is explicitly not one protocol, not software-only, and not a single vendor's platform.

questions.question: By 2026 the slides report machine traffic at 53% versus 47% human, having crossed 50% in 2024. What is cited as the main cause of the recent rise in bot traffic?
options: Wider rollout of 5G networks
Adoption of Generative AI
Growth in online video streaming
Expansion of smart metering programs
questions.explanation: The Imperva Bad Bot figures attribute the increase in bot traffic primarily to the adoption of Generative AI. The other items are real trends but are not named as the driver of the bot-traffic shift.

questions.question: The ITU view of IoT as available 'anywhere, anytime, by anything and anyone' chiefly expresses which property?
options: Ubiquity / pervasiveness of connected things
Cryptographic security of the network
Centralized control of all devices
Low energy consumption of endpoints
questions.explanation: The phrase captures ubiquity — pervasive availability across places, times and actors. It is not a statement about security, centralization or power efficiency.

questions.question: Across mobile generations, why is 5G — rather than 4G — the generation explicitly associated with IoT in the comparison table?
options: 5G is analog and therefore better suited to sensors
5G's far higher bandwidth (up to ~10 Gb/s) supports the massive density and data volumes of connected things, whereas 4G's main application is video streaming
4G cannot transmit any data, only voice
5G eliminates the need for any protocol standardization
questions.explanation: The table maps each generation to a main application: 4G to video streaming and 5G to the Internet of Things, enabled by 5G's much higher bandwidth supporting device density and throughput. 5G is digital, 4G clearly carries data, and 5G does not remove standardization needs.

questions.question: In the ITU enabling-technologies framing, sensors and actuators play complementary roles. Which pairing is correct?
options: Sensors are output 'hands' that act; actuators are input 'eyes' that observe
Sensors are input 'eyes' that collect information; actuators are output 'hands' that implement decisions
Both sensors and actuators only collect information
Both sensors and actuators only implement decisions
questions.explanation: The slides cast sensors as input devices ('eyes' that collect information) and actuators as output units ('hands' that implement decisions). The complementarity — sensing then acting — is what lets IoT close the loop between observation and action.

questions.question: Why are smart materials singled out as a distinct enabling category rather than just sensors or just actuators?
options: They contain neither sensors nor actuators but store data
They incorporate both sensors and actuators and can be passive, active or autonomous
They are purely decorative and have no IoT function
They only work when wired to a central server
questions.explanation: Smart materials are described as incorporating both sensors and actuators, and can be passive, active or autonomous. That fusion of sensing and acting within the material itself is what distinguishes them.

questions.question: RFID is presented as having an advantage over barcode technologies for tagging things. What is the practical basis for that advantage?
options: RFID requires direct line of sight like a camera
RFID can be read without line of sight and supports unique identification of individual items
RFID is always cheaper than a printed barcode
RFID stores no identifying information at all
questions.explanation: RFID's edge over barcodes lies in readability without line of sight and unique item-level identification, which suits large-scale automated tagging. Barcodes need line of sight; RFID is not always cheaper; and RFID exists precisely to carry identifying data.

questions.question: Among the protocols listed, which is classified as general-purpose rather than specific to IoT?
options: Zigbee
Z-Wave
Wi-Fi
LoRaWAN
questions.explanation: The protocol table marks Wi-Fi (along with 6LoWPAN, Thread, cellular, NFC) as general-purpose, while Zigbee, Z-Wave, Sigfox, Neul and LoRaWAN are specific to IoT. The distinction matters because mixing IoT-specific and general-purpose stacks is part of the interoperability problem.

questions.question: The ITU groups enabling technologies by function: tagging, feeling, thinking, shrinking. Which mapping is correct?
options: Tagging = nanotechnology; shrinking = RFID
Feeling = sensor technologies; shrinking = nanotechnology
Thinking = RFID; feeling = smart technologies
Shrinking = sensors; thinking = nanotechnology
questions.explanation: The mapping is: tagging = RFID, feeling = sensor technologies, thinking = smart technologies, shrinking = nanotechnology. Only the pairing of feeling with sensors and shrinking with nanotechnology is internally consistent.

questions.question: Why does the large variety of IoT frameworks, architectures and protocols create the interoperability challenge highlighted in the slides?
options: Because all standards are identical and therefore redundant
Because fragmented and often siloed standards make it hard for heterogeneous devices to work together, prompting consortia to form
Because there is only one global standard and no alternatives
Because interoperability is irrelevant once devices are connected
questions.explanation: Supply-side complexity — many frameworks, OS, protocols, industry-specific versus general-purpose and open versus proprietary choices — fragments the landscape, which is exactly why consortia like the Open Connectivity Foundation, oneM2M and Thread Group work on interoperability.

questions.question: Why are IoT security challenges considered to intensify specifically as deployments scale up?
options: Larger networks automatically become more secure
The sheer number of devices and transactions, network complexity, device anonymity and access/authentication and identity-management difficulties compound at scale
Security only depends on the presence of Wi-Fi
Scaling removes the need for identity management
questions.explanation: The slides list the causes of IoT security challenges as the number of devices, number of transactions, network complexity, device 'anonymity', access and authentication, and identity management. These do not shrink with scale — they compound, which is why scale aggravates security.

questions.question: Why is identity management an especially acute problem in IoT compared with traditional IT?
options: IoT devices never need to communicate
Devices are effectively anonymous and access/authentication become difficult to manage across a very large number of endpoints
Identity management only applies to paper records
IoT devices each have a permanent human operator
questions.explanation: Device 'anonymity' plus access and authentication across enormous device counts make identity management hard. The other options contradict how IoT works — devices do communicate and rarely have a dedicated human operator.

questions.question: In the Edge–Core–Endpoints architecture, what do 'endpoints' refer to?
options: Designated computing datacenters on premises and in the cloud
Enterprise servers and appliances located outside the datacenters
Terminal devices such as PCs, smartphones, sensors and wearables
The cryptographic keys used to sign transactions
questions.explanation: Endpoints are the terminal devices: PCs, smartphones, sensors and wearables. Core refers to datacenters and all cloud forms; Edge refers to enterprise servers and appliances not in the datacenter.

questions.question: The 'Core' tier in the IoT architecture is best described as:
options: Terminal devices like wearables and sensors
Designated computing datacenters on premises and in the cloud, covering private, public and hybrid cloud
Enterprise appliances at the network edge outside the datacenter
The set of communication protocols only
questions.explanation: Core denotes the designated computing datacenters — on premises and in the cloud — and explicitly spans private, public and hybrid cloud. Endpoints are terminal devices; Edge sits outside the datacenter.

questions.question: The IEEE describes the long-term IoT technology challenge as 'shifting intelligence.' What does this mean in practice and why is it pursued?
options: Removing all computing from devices and centralizing it in one datacenter
Devolving information-processing capability toward the edges of the network so embedded intelligence enhances overall network power
Returning all processing to paper-based systems
Eliminating sensors so devices only transmit raw signals
questions.explanation: The IEEE position is that embedded intelligence in the things themselves, by devolving processing to the edges, enhances the power of the network. This is the rationale for edge computing — the opposite of full centralization or removing intelligence from devices.

questions.question: Why is 'availability of adjacent technologies' listed as an internal factor influencing IoT adoption?
options: Because IoT works in complete isolation from other technologies
Because IoT depends on complementary technologies being in place for it to deliver value
Because adjacent technologies are competitors that must be blocked
Because it determines the colour of the device casing
questions.explanation: Adoption is shaped by whether complementary, adjacent technologies are available to support IoT use. IoT is not isolated; complementarity is an enabler, not a competitive threat, and has nothing to do with cosmetic attributes.

questions.question: Why is 'ease of use' treated as an intrinsic factor in technology adoption for IoT and blockchain?
options: It is unrelated to whether people and organizations actually adopt the technology
Lower friction in using the technology directly raises the likelihood and speed of adoption
It only matters for marketing brochures
It guarantees the technology is energy-efficient
questions.explanation: Ease of use lowers the barrier to adoption, which is why it sits among intrinsic adoption factors alongside standards, interoperability and availability of adjacent technologies. It is an adoption driver, not a marketing detail or an energy property.

questions.question: Connected cars are described as 'computers on wheels.' Why does this framing raise a strategic question for manufacturers?
options: Because cars no longer need any hardware
Because it opens the question of which operating system will dominate and whether carmakers build their own software or rely on existing platforms
Because software is irrelevant to modern vehicles
Because it eliminates all competition in the automotive sector
questions.explanation: Treating cars as computers on wheels surfaces the discussion points in the slides: the dominant OS for cars, how many software applications already exist, and whether manufacturers create their own software or depend on platforms such as Android Automotive OS. It is a question about software strategy, not the absence of hardware.

questions.question: Smart-mobility P2P carpooling is distinguished from services like Uber and Lyft on what basis?
options: It requires a larger intermediation platform than Uber
Relationships are 1-to-1 (peer-to-peer) with no need for an intermediation platform in the middle
It only works for freight, not passengers
It is fully controlled by a central dispatch authority
questions.explanation: The slides define smart mobility as P2P applications for carpooling and on-demand car sharing where relationships are 1-2-1 and there is no need for an intermediation platform — the key contrast with platform-mediated Uber/Lyft. IoT acts as the enabler of direct peer interaction.

questions.question: Smart metering records consumption in intervals of an hour or less and reports it to the utility. Why is data collection a central discussion point for this use case?
options: Because the data has no commercial or personal value
Because fine-grained consumption data raises privacy and regulation concerns while also enabling value creation
Because meters cannot transmit any data
Because regulation forbids any data collection entirely
questions.explanation: The discussion points for smart metering are roll-out/adoption rate, data collection and privacy (regulation), and data usage (value creation). Granular data is simultaneously a privacy/regulatory issue and a source of value — not valueless, and the meters explicitly do transmit data.

questions.question: For the smart-home use case (real-time adaptation of blinds, lights, cooling based on humidity, occupancy and natural light), which question is flagged as a primary discussion point?
options: The brand of the light bulbs
Ownership of the data and ownership of the IoT system
The colour temperature of the display
The number of Wi-Fi channels available
questions.explanation: The smart-home discussion points are ownership of data and ownership of the IoT system — governance questions about who controls the generated data and the platform, not cosmetic or purely technical radio details.

questions.question: Which set correctly lists macro-level IoT use cases presented in the course?
options: Email encryption, password hashing, NFT minting
Smart Home, Smart City, Smart Transportation/Mobility
Server virtualization, browser caching, OCR
Audio compression, image rendering, web indexing
questions.explanation: The summary cites Smart Home, Smart City and Smart Transportation as macro-level IoT use cases. The other lists are unrelated computing tasks, not IoT use cases.

questions.question: In the case-study themes, which mapping of theme to interaction type is correct?
options: Industry 4.0 = B2C consumer IoT
Industry 4.0 = B2B industrial IoT; Smart Homes = B2C consumer IoT
Smart Mobility = paper-based identity systems
Smart Cities = offline photo editing
questions.explanation: The themes map Industry 4.0 to B2B industrial IoT and Smart Homes to B2C consumer IoT, with human-to-machine and machine-to-machine patterns across the rest. The other options pair themes with unrelated activities.

questions.question: Ben Green's 'Smart Enough Cities' critique is cited as an external (non-technical) factor. What is the substance of the critique?
options: Cities should be optimized purely with more sensors and algorithms
Treating cities as abstract technical processes to be optimized risks ignoring the fundamental social and political challenges of urban life
Smart cities are technically impossible to build
Privacy is never a concern in urban deployments
questions.explanation: Green warns against framing cities as abstract technical processes optimized by sensors, data and algorithms while sidestepping the social and political challenges of urban life. The critique is precisely against a sensor-only, optimization-first view.

questions.question: The slides discuss a 'dark side' of IoT through examples like firms tracking employees' keystrokes and mouse clicks. Why are these raised?
options: To showcase IoT's entertainment value
To highlight ethical concerns such as workplace surveillance and exploitative digital labour used to train AI
To demonstrate that IoT has no social downsides
To prove that IoT only operates offline
questions.explanation: The 'dark side' examples — keystroke tracking to train AI models and platform 'digital labour' — are raised to surface ethical concerns around surveillance and low-paid digital work. They illustrate downsides, not benefits or offline operation.

questions.question: Shapiro and Varian's classification of switching costs is invoked to explain why technology change is often resisted. What is the underlying argument?
options: Switching is always free, so adoption is instant
The cost of change (lock-in plus switching costs) is frequently a decisive decision element and a potential barrier to change
Switching costs only matter for hardware, never data
Lock-in disappears once a contract is signed
questions.explanation: Shapiro and Varian argue that the cost of change — combining lock-in and switching costs — is often an important decision element and therefore a barrier to change. This explains slow adoption even of superior technologies; switching is rarely free.

questions.question: Which lock-in type is correctly paired with its associated switching cost?
options: Loyalty programs — learning costs
Information and databases — costs of converting data to new formats
Specific skill set — cancellation costs
Durable equipment — loss of acquired advantages
questions.explanation: Information and databases are paired with the cost of converting data to new formats. The correct pairings elsewhere are: loyalty programs → loss of acquired advantages; specific skill set → learning costs; durable equipment → replacement costs; contracts → cancellation costs.

questions.question: Why would a 'specialized suppliers' lock-in deter a firm from switching technologies?
options: Because the cost lies in changing suppliers when the new technology requires different ones
Because specialized suppliers are always free to replace
Because suppliers have no influence on technology choice
Because it only affects loyalty-program points
questions.explanation: The switching cost tied to specialized suppliers is the cost of changing suppliers — replacing relationships and dependencies built around the current technology. That friction is what makes the lock-in deter change.

questions.question: Among Shapiro and Varian's seven standard-setting factors, why is 'installed base' so frequently decisive?
options: A large installed base creates momentum and network effects that pull further adoption toward the same standard
A large installed base makes a technology obsolete faster
Installed base only matters for hardware colour choices
Installed base is irrelevant once IP rights exist
questions.explanation: Installed base is the first of the seven factors because an existing user base generates momentum and network effects, drawing further adoption toward the established standard (the QWERTY example illustrates this). It is a driver of dominance, not obsolescence.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the seven standard-setting factors listed by Shapiro and Varian?
options: IP rights
Pioneer's advantage
Tax policy
Brand reputation
questions.explanation: The seven factors are installed base, IP rights, capacity to innovate, pioneer's advantage, production capacity, product complementarity and brand reputation. Tax policy is not among them.

questions.question: In the standard-setting strategy map, when there is conflict between players the slide notes that the weak tends to:
options: Immediately surrender to the strong
Block the strong, leading to a 'standard war'
Avoid all compatibility issues automatically
Eliminate the installed base of the strong
questions.explanation: Under conflict, the choice of the weak is to block the strong, producing a 'standard war'; agreement on a standard is the alternative outcome. The weak does not automatically surrender or erase the strong's installed base.

questions.question: Among generic strategies for launching a new technology, what does choosing 'compatibility' (controlled or open migration) trade off against?
options: It trades off against 'performance', which implies discontinuity from the existing base
It trades off against lowering production capacity
It trades off against brand reputation only
It has no trade-off; it dominates all other choices
questions.explanation: The strategy grid contrasts compatibility (controlled migration / open migration) with performance (discontinuity). Backward compatibility eases migration but constrains performance, while a performance leap implies discontinuity from the installed base — a genuine trade-off.

questions.question: Why might a firm choose 'openness / open migration' over 'control' when launching a new technology in a network market?
options: To restrict the technology to a single licensee
To accelerate adoption and grow the installed base by lowering barriers, at the cost of tighter proprietary control
To guarantee the highest possible per-unit price
To avoid having any installed base at all
questions.explanation: Openness lowers barriers and can rapidly build the installed base and network effects, trading away the tighter appropriation that control offers. The choice is fundamentally about adoption speed versus proprietary control.

questions.question: Porter and Heppelmann argue that smart, connected products are strategically significant. Why?
options: They have no effect on how value is created or captured
They raise new choices about how value is created and captured, how data is utilized and managed, how partner relationships are redefined, and how industry boundaries expand
They only matter for personal entertainment
They automatically remove all channel partners
questions.explanation: The Porter/Heppelmann quote stresses new strategic choices on value creation and capture, management of large amounts of sensitive data, redefinition of partner (e.g., channel) relationships, and expanding industry boundaries. They reshape strategy rather than being entertainment or automatically eliminating partners.

questions.question: Why is a blockchain considered resistant to modification of its data?
options: Because each block is stored on a single secured server
Because each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block plus a timestamp and transaction data, so altering one block breaks the chain
Because the data is never written to disk
Because a central administrator approves every edit
questions.explanation: Each block embeds the cryptographic hash of the previous block, a timestamp and transaction data; tampering with any block invalidates all subsequent hashes, making modification detectable. There is deliberately no central administrator, and the data is persisted across many nodes.

questions.question: A blockchain block typically contains which combination of elements?
options: A user interface, image files and a password list
A cryptographic hash of the previous block, a timestamp and transaction data
A single central server address and nothing else
Only the current account balances
questions.explanation: By design a block holds the hash of the previous block, a timestamp and transaction data (often as a Merkle tree). The other options describe artefacts that are not the structure of a block.

questions.question: A distributed ledger (DLT) differs from a centralized database in what essential way?
options: It is controlled by a single administrator at one site
It is a consensus of replicated, shared and synchronized data spread across multiple sites with no central administrator
It can only be stored on smartphones
It is a temporary cache that is erased after each transaction
questions.explanation: A DLT is a consensus of replicated, shared and synchronized digital data spread across sites, countries or institutions, and crucially has no central administrator — the defining contrast with a centralized database.

questions.question: In blockchain, the role of the 'trusted third party' is said to become 'the system itself.' What makes this possible?
options: A bank validates each transaction off-chain
Each distributed block contains the information that guarantees data integrity through a cryptographic algorithm
A human notary signs every block manually
A cloud password manager stores the trust credentials
questions.explanation: Trust shifts from an external entity to the system because each block in the distributed chain carries the information that guarantees integrity of exchanged data via cryptography. No bank, manual notary or password manager is required.

questions.question: Why is a peer-to-peer (P2P) relationship foundational to blockchain rather than a client-server one?
options: Because one privileged server must coordinate all peers
Because peers are equally privileged, equipotent nodes that partition tasks among themselves without a central coordinator
Because P2P requires constant human messaging
Because P2P only works for broadcast television
questions.explanation: P2P networking partitions tasks among peers that are equally privileged and equipotent (the Napster example), which underpins blockchain's lack of a central coordinator. A privileged central server would contradict the architecture.

questions.question: In the centralized–decentralized–distributed distinction, why is a distributed architecture more resistant to single points of failure?
options: Because control and data sit on one master node
Because data and control are replicated and synchronized across many nodes, so no single node is essential
Because it runs entirely offline
Because it forbids any replication of data
questions.explanation: A distributed system replicates and synchronizes across many independent nodes, removing the single chokepoint that a centralized (one master) design has. Replication is the source of resilience, not something the architecture forbids.

questions.question: Iansiti and Lakhani compare blockchain to TCP/IP. What is the basis of that analogy?
options: Both are sensor protocols for IoT devices
Just as TCP/IP dramatically lowered the cost of connections, blockchain could dramatically lower the cost of transactions and become a system of record
Both are mobile operating systems
Both eliminate the need for any cryptography
questions.explanation: The HBR argument is that TCP/IP unlocked value by lowering connection costs, and blockchain could similarly lower transaction costs and become the system of record for all transactions, triggering a comparable economic shift. The analogy is economic and infrastructural.

questions.question: Why is blockchain described as an 'infrastructural' technology in the summary?
options: Because it is only useful as a consumer app
Because, like TCP/IP for communication networks, it can serve as a foundational layer on which many digital services are built
Because it must run on dedicated physical cables
Because it replaces the need for the Internet entirely
questions.explanation: The summary frames blockchain as infrastructural: 'Blockchain is to digital services what TCP/IP is for communication networks' — a base layer enabling many services, not a single consumer app nor a wholesale replacement for the Internet.

questions.question: Which trio correctly lists blockchain application domains shown in the course?
options: Image compression, voice recognition, web indexing
Asset transfer, traceability, automatic execution of contracts
Spreadsheet formatting, cabling, weather forecasting
Keyboard optimization, OCR, audio mixing
questions.explanation: The application-domains slide names asset transfer, traceability and automatic execution of contracts (smart contracts). The other lists are unrelated computing tasks.

questions.question: Why does a smart contract remove the need for a human intermediary, using the 'immediate refund if a plane is delayed' insurance example?
options: Because a claims adjuster manually reviews each flight
Because the contract executes automatically when predefined conditions are met, without arbitration by a central authority
Because passengers must call the airline to trigger it
Because it only works on paper contracts
questions.explanation: Smart contracts are about automatic execution: when the triggering condition (flight delay) is verified, the refund executes without manual intervention or a central arbiter. That self-execution is what displaces the intermediary.

questions.question: Why are NFTs 'non-fungible,' and how does that distinguish them from cryptocurrencies?
options: They are fully interchangeable, exactly like one bitcoin for another
They are pieces of code tied to a specific digital asset (with a license to use/copy/display) and are not mutually interchangeable, unlike fungible cryptocurrencies
They are anonymous packets of sensor data
They are private keys for Wi-Fi access
questions.explanation: An NFT is code associated with a digital asset, usually with a license to use, copy or display it; because each is unique and not mutually interchangeable, it is non-fungible — the opposite of interchangeable cryptocurrency units.

questions.question: Why does blockchain enable peer-to-peer energy trading between individual producers?
options: Because it forces all energy through the central distribution network
Because it lets producers (often of renewable energy) trade directly with one another without going through the central distribution network
Because it generates electricity itself
Because it bans renewable energy sources
questions.explanation: Blockchain-enabled energy trading allows individuals — often renewable producers — to trade energy directly, bypassing the central distribution network. Blockchain is the enabler of the P2P interaction, not a power generator.

questions.question: In food-product traceability, why is blockchain positioned as a 'source of trust'?
options: Because it hides the origin of products
Because it provides a single, tamper-resistant source of information on origin, ingredients, transformation, transport and distribution, improving supply-chain transparency
Because it slows down the supply chain deliberately
Because it only records the final retail price
questions.explanation: Traceability uses blockchain to give a unique, reliable record across the food chain — origin, ingredients, transformation, transport, intermediaries and distribution — which is exactly what makes it a source of trust and transparency.

questions.question: In the luxury industry (e.g., the Aura Blockchain Consortium), what is blockchain/NFT primarily used for and at what adoption stage?
options: Mass production, at full maturity
Digital passports and anti-counterfeiting collectibles, still at an early adoption stage relative to 3D printing and RFID
Replacing all physical stores, at peak adoption
Energy generation, at the decline stage
questions.explanation: Aura groups luxury brands around digital passports and NFT collectibles, an anti-counterfeit use; the Comité Colbert/Bain study places blockchain (mainly NFT) in early adoption compared with 3D printing and RFID. It is an authentication use case, not mass production or energy.

questions.question: Among blockchain's main application types, which concrete example is correctly matched?
options: Smart contracts — image compression
Cryptocurrencies — liquid stock exchange via security tokens
Distributed ledgers — keyboard layout optimization
Anti-counterfeiting/NFT — Wi-Fi roaming
questions.explanation: The overview matches application types to concrete cases: cryptocurrencies/security tokens to a liquid stock exchange, smart contracts to immediate insurance refunds, traceability to food markets, and NFT to tokenized artwork and game assets. Only the cryptocurrency/security-token pairing is correct here.

questions.question: Why is scalability listed as an internal blockchain adoption challenge?
options: Because blockchain handles far more transactions per second than traditional networks
Because a blockchain network enables a relatively lower number of transactions per second compared with traditional transaction networks
Because it cannot store any transactions
Because it requires no processing power
questions.explanation: Scalability is a challenge precisely because blockchain networks process relatively fewer transactions per second than conventional networks, limiting throughput for high-volume uses.

questions.question: Why does interoperability remain a challenge across blockchain networks?
options: Because all blockchains are designed to interconnect seamlessly by default
Because most blockchain networks are designed to work in silo mode
Because blockchains never store digital data
Because they only operate with barcodes
questions.explanation: Most blockchain networks are built to operate in silo mode, so they do not naturally interoperate — the opposite of seamless interconnection. This fragmentation is the interoperability challenge.

questions.question: Why is energy consumption a notable blockchain adoption challenge?
options: Because transaction validation requires a large amount of processing power
Because blockchain runs entirely on paper
Because it cannot store timestamps
Because it uses only analog hardware
questions.explanation: Validating transactions demands significant processing power, which translates into high energy consumption — a recognized barrier, also reflected in concerns about NFTs and cryptocurrencies.

questions.question: Why is 'talent' counted among blockchain adoption challenges?
options: Because blockchain requires no specialized knowledge
Because trained blockchain specialists are scarce and the field demands interdisciplinarity
Because talent only affects marketing
Because it concerns the physical size of offices
questions.explanation: The slides list talent as a challenge due to the shortage of trained blockchain specialists and the need for interdisciplinary skills. It is a human-capital constraint, not a marketing or facilities matter.

questions.question: A SYN flood attack weakens blockchain security by which mechanism?
options: Splitting the network into isolated groups
Sending requests rapidly and repeatedly until the target is overwhelmed and lacks the processing power to legitimize and control traffic
Controlling a majority of mining nodes
Intercepting and silently modifying valid transactions
questions.explanation: A SYN flood overwhelms the target with rapid, repeated requests so it no longer has enough processing power to validate and control traffic. Network splitting describes an Eclipse attack, node control a Sybil attack, and interception a man-in-the-middle attack.

questions.question: What characterizes a Sybil attack on a blockchain network?
options: A user simply forgets a password
An attacker gains influence by controlling multiple nodes (and their associated miners), forming a network of colluding participants
A device runs out of battery
A block becomes too large to transmit
questions.explanation: In a Sybil attack the attacker accesses the network through nodes they control, with the associated miners being their own, creating a network of 'traffickers' that facilitates further attacks. It is about controlling many identities/nodes, not a forgotten password or hardware failure.

questions.question: Why is an Eclipse attack problematic for a blockchain network?
options: It speeds up all transactions uniformly
It splits the network into separate groups so users in one group cannot join another and parallel chains grow independently
It automatically executes smart contracts
It recovers energy lost during mining
questions.explanation: An Eclipse attack causes the network to split into groups that cannot communicate, so chains grow separately; awareness of another group requires receiving a block from an unknown chain. It fragments consensus rather than improving performance.

questions.question: Why can a man-in-the-middle attack succeed in inserting invalid transactions on a blockchain?
options: Because every transaction is audited in real time by a regulator
Because, since valid transactions are not audited, a hacker who intercepts and modifies information can insert invalid transactions that appear valid
Because the attacker physically destroys the nodes
Because blockchains store no transaction data
questions.explanation: The slide notes that because valid transactions are not audited, an attacker intercepting and modifying information can slip invalid transactions that appear valid into the ledger. The vulnerability stems from the lack of auditing, not regulator review or physical destruction.

questions.question: Roubini's 'dark side' critique argues that blockchain decentralization is largely a myth. What evidence is cited for that view?
options: All mining is evenly distributed among millions of small participants
A handful of companies control most mining, and crypto trading runs on centralized exchanges that are frequently hacked
Blockchain has eliminated every security risk
Decentralized governance is fully transparent everywhere
questions.explanation: Roubini points out that decision-making is often centralized and opaque, a few 'anonymous cartels' control most mining, and crypto trading occurs on centralized exchanges that are frequently hacked — undercutting the decentralization claim. The other options describe the idealized view he criticizes.

questions.question: Why is blockchain adoption outside cryptocurrencies described as relatively slow?
options: Because it is already universal across all sectors
Because of inherent complexity, transparency/trust issues, and the difficulty of embedding existing legal provisions at the technology layer
Because it has no real-world applications
Because it requires no legal or organizational adaptation
questions.explanation: The summary attributes slow non-crypto adoption to inherent complexity, transparency (trust) challenges, and the difficulty of embedding existing legal provisions at the technology layer. It is neither universal nor free of legal adaptation needs.

questions.question: Why might combining IoT and blockchain (IBM's 'device democracy' idea) be attractive?
options: To make IoT fully centralized under one vendor
To address IoT's scaling and trust challenges by using a distributed, tamper-resistant ledger among devices
To remove all data generation from IoT
To replace sensors with cryptocurrency tokens
questions.explanation: The 'device democracy' approach pairs IoT's data generation and scale with blockchain's distributed trust to tackle scaling and trust problems in large device networks. It is about decentralized trust, not centralization or removing IoT's core functions.

questions.question: In the simple IoT/Blockchain value-chain model, what is the role of the sensor at the start of the chain?
options: It performs final data visualization for executives
It acts as the source of data/information that the rest of the chain collects, transmits, processes and feeds back to actuators
It stores the entire distributed ledger
It replaces the networking layer
questions.explanation: In the model the sensor is the source of data/information; the chain then handles data collection, connectivity/networking, processing, and feedback to actuators. The sensor originates data rather than visualizing it or storing the ledger.

questions.question: The value-creation-through-data steps are ordered for a reason. Which sequence matches the model?
options: Insights → analytics → integration → collection
Data collection → cleansing/preparation → integration of several sources → analytics → visualization → insights and recommendations
Analytics → collection → insights → cleansing
Visualization → collection → recommendations → integration
questions.explanation: Value creation through data follows collection, then cleansing/preparation, then integration of several sources, then analytics, then (optionally) visualization, and finally insights and recommendations. The ordering matters because each stage depends on the quality of the prior one.

questions.question: In the European regulatory landscape for IoT and blockchain, which is correctly classified?
options: GDPR is only a draft proposal
GDPR is an existing regulation, while the E-Privacy Regulation and Free Flow of Data Regulation are noted as proposed/draft
PSD2 was never enacted
The NIS Directive is purely hypothetical
questions.explanation: The slides list GDPR (May 2018), the NIS Directive and PSD2 as existing regulations, and the E-Privacy Regulation and Free Flow of Data Regulation as proposed/draft. GDPR is in force, not a draft.

questions.question: The wrap-up uses examples like DC vs AC electricity and the QWERTY keyboard. What general adoption lesson do these illustrate?
options: That superior technologies always win immediately on merit
That standards, installed base and the co-existence or rivalry of technologies shape adoption beyond pure technical merit
That technology adoption is unrelated to history or installed base
That only government mandates determine standards
questions.explanation: The examples show that installed base (QWERTY), standards, convergence of different knowledge, and the co-existence of initially rival technologies (DC and AC) drive adoption — outcomes are not decided by technical superiority alone.

questions.question: Why does the course conclude that both IoT and blockchain should be carefully assessed before society-wide implementation?
options: Because they are simple technologies with no trade-offs
Because each combines several technologies and raises technical, ethical, regulatory and trust considerations whose impacts at societal scale are significant
Because neither has any real use case
Because assessment is only needed for entertainment products
questions.explanation: The summary stresses careful assessment, especially for society-wide initiatives, because both are composite technologies (combining many sub-technologies) with security, privacy, energy, legal and trust implications that scale with deployment. They are neither trivial nor use-case-free.

questions.question: Why is blockchain summarized as being 'about trust (and control)' while IoT is summarized as a 'data generation technology set'?
options: Because both phrases mean exactly the same thing
Because blockchain's core contribution is establishing trust without an intermediary, whereas IoT's core contribution is generating data by combining sensing technologies
Because IoT is about trust and blockchain is about sensors
Because neither technology relates to data
questions.explanation: The summary contrasts the two: blockchain is fundamentally about trust and control via a distributed ledger used (outside crypto) for P2P transactions, while IoT is a data generation technology set combining RFID, sensors, smart and nano technologies. The framings are deliberately distinct.

questions.question: Why are privacy and personal-data collection treated as primary external factors when implementing IoT 'solutions' to real-world problems?
options: Because IoT never collects any personal data
Because mass sensing raises privacy, personal-data collection and surveillance concerns that are non-technical yet decisive for acceptance
Because privacy only matters for paper records
Because external factors have no effect on adoption
questions.explanation: The slides flag privacy, personal-data collection and mass surveillance as primary considerations — non-technical (sociological, cultural, organizational) factors that strongly shape whether IoT solutions are accepted. They are external adoption factors, not irrelevant ones.

questions.question: Why does the course emphasize 'combinatorial effects of technologies' (WEF/Accenture) when discussing IoT and blockchain?
options: Because each technology delivers maximum value only in isolation
Because much of digital transformation's value arises from combining technologies, so their joint effects exceed what any one delivers alone
Because combining technologies always reduces value
Because combination is only relevant to hardware pricing
questions.explanation: The combinatorial-effects framing (securing large societal/industry value) argues that combining digital technologies multiplies impact — IoT and blockchain among them — rather than each working best alone. Combination amplifies rather than reduces value.

questions.question: Why is connectivity/networking a necessary middle stage in the IoT value chain rather than an optional add-on?
options: Because sensors can deliver value without ever transmitting data
Because data captured at the endpoint must be transmitted and networked before it can be processed and acted upon elsewhere
Because networking replaces the need for sensors and actuators
Because connectivity is only used for billing
questions.explanation: In the model, data is collected at the point of capture and must move through connectivity/networking to reach processing and ultimately feedback to actuators. Without transmission the data cannot be aggregated, processed or acted on, so connectivity is integral, not optional.
